full_story_text:
A small slider inside the refrigerator may seem like a detail no one needs to think about. But that little choice can change the air around fresh food—and how quickly some of it loses quality.

Many refrigerators have two settings in the produce drawer: low humidity and high humidity. The low setting lets more air move through. The high setting keeps more moisture inside.

At first, this sounds like a simple fruit-versus-vegetable choice. It is not.

Fresh produce does not face the same storage problem. Some food needs protection from water loss. Some can affect nearby food as it matures. That is why the labels need a closer look.

The produce drawer is more than a box for food. It is a small storage system. The useful question is not only what the food is called, but what may happen after it goes inside.
point_one_text:
Match the setting to the problem
For refrigerated produce, ask which problem matters more: ethylene exposure for nearby food or fast moisture loss that causes wilting. Apples and pears fit the first group and suit the ventilated low-humidity side. Kale and broccoli fit the second and suit the high-humidity side. This replaces a misleading fruit-versus-vegetable guess with a spoilage check.
point_two_text:
Check the storage place first
Before choosing a setting, ask whether the food belongs in the refrigerator at all. Tomatoes and bananas are recommended for counter storage. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic need a cool, dry place instead. For strawberries and oranges, household guidance is not universal. If official sources or appliance makers differ, check the instructions for your own refrigerator model instead of assuming one setting fits all.
